newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile blasts Russia over Mars space probe secrecy.
newsitem.headline: Chile blasts Russia over Mars space probe secrecy.

text.p: Chile attacked Russia on Monday over its reluctance to release information to help in the search for the ill-fated Mars 96 space probe which may have plunged to earth over the northern part of the country.
"We still don't have all the information available," Chilean Defence Minister Edmundo Perez said. "The Russian authorities have been tremendously unwilling to give precise information."

The satellite, which was carrying eight ounces (200 grams) of plutonium, crashed back to earth two weeks ago sparking fears of an environmental disaster if any of the highly radioactive plutonium leaked.

Although most of the probe was thought to have been destroyed on re-entry, the U.S. space agency said last week a piece of the satellite could have fallen in a 1,100 mile (1,800 km) area covering land and sea in northern Chile.
The satellite was originally thought to have crashed hundreds of miles further west into the Pacific Ocean between the remote Easter Island and the Chilean mainland.
Perez said Chile does not have enough information to evaluate the risk of a leak of the plutonium which was contained in the rocket's four tiny batteries.
"Unfortunately we do not have enough information at the moment, although we know that the container in which the plutonium was stored resists very strong impacts," he said.
Chile's air force and navy will continue searching for traces of radioactivity and wreckage from the probe, he said.
So far the tests, which have included air and water samples, have not shown any signs of radiation, said military officials.

Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza said the Russian authorities have reassured Chile that there is no danger of contamination as the batteries were designed to withstand the heat and stress of landing on Mars.
"We have received new assurances from the Russian government that ... there is no danger of any type from the radioactive material," he said. "But naturally we must verify this."
Environmentalists have said any radioactive contamination in the sea could devastate rich fishing grounds in the southern Pacific which attract trawlers from around the world.
The doomed Mars-96 rocket fell back to earth just a day after take-off when a booster rocket misfired, preventing the craft from breaking free of the Earth's gravity.
